title: Vākyapadīya
summary: Bhartṛhari's treatise on 'sentence and word' in three books. Book 1 (Brahmakāṇḍa) teaches that Brahman is the Word-principle appearing as the world, that all cognition is word-permeated, the sphoṭa–dhvani distinction, the three levels of speech and grammar as a path to liberation; book 2 (Vākyakāṇḍa) argues that the sentence is the indivisible unit of meaning, grasped as pratibhā; book 3 (Padakāṇḍa or Prakīrṇaka) analyses universals, substance, relation, quality, direction, means, action, time, person, number, gender and compounds in fourteen sections (samuddeśa).

attribution.tradition: Bhartṛhari (often identified in the tradition with the poet of the Śatakatraya)
attribution.scholarly: Bhartṛhari the grammarian; his identity with the poet of the Śatakas is doubted

scholarly.text: c. 5th c. CE (before Dignāga, who uses it)

structure.description: 3 kāṇḍas; kāṇḍa 3 in 14 samuddeśas (jāti, dravya, sambandha, bhūyodravya, guṇa, dik, sādhana, kriyā, kāla, puruṣa, saṃkhyā, upagraha, liṅga, vṛtti); roughly 2,000 kārikās (count differs by edition)

editions.name: ed. K. A. Subramania Iyer (Poona, 1963–1973, with Vṛtti and commentaries)
ed. W. Rau (Wiesbaden, 1977; critical text of the kārikās)
K. A. Subramania Iyer, English translation (kāṇḍas 1–3)

notes: Vākyapadīya numbering follows K. A. Subramania Iyer's edition; W. Rau's edition numbers kāṇḍa 1 differently after about v. 30, so the locator may need conversion. Not present in the local sources_raw mirror at Phase B.

title: Vākyapadīya-vṛtti (Svopajñavṛtti)
summary: The prose commentary on books 1 and 2 of the Vākyapadīya, which explains the three levels of speech with verses defining vaikharī, madhyamā and paśyantī, the yoga of the word (śabdapūrva-yoga) and grammar's place among the sciences.

attribution.scholarly: most accept Bhartṛhari's authorship; some have proposed another author (Harivṛṣabha)

title: Paddhati (Sphuṭākṣarā) of Vṛṣabhadeva
summary: Vṛṣabhadeva's sub-commentary on the Vṛtti to book 1 of the Vākyapadīya; an important early witness to how the Brahmakāṇḍa was read.

title: Ṭīkā on the Vākyakāṇḍa ascribed to Puṇyarāja
summary: A commentary on book 2 of the Vākyapadīya (and in some editions on book 1) transmitted under Puṇyarāja's name, the main guide to the Vākyakāṇḍa's theory of the sentence and pratibhā.

attribution.scholarly: the ascription is debated; parts may derive from Helārāja

title: Prakīrṇaprakāśa of Helārāja
summary: Helārāja's commentary on book 3 of the Vākyapadīya, reading the analysis of universals, substance, time and the other categories in the light of the Word-monism; Helārāja refers to his (lost) commentary Śabdaprabhā on the first books.

title: Mahābhāṣya-dīpikā (Tripādī) of Bhartṛhari
summary: Bhartṛhari's commentary on Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya, the earliest known, surviving in a single damaged manuscript that covers only part of the first book of Pāṇini.

title: Vyākaraṇa-Mahābhāṣya
summary: U31 contribution: for the grammarian-philosophers the Mahābhāṣya supplies the founding questions — what the word is (the Paspaśā's answer: that by whose utterance the thing is understood), the eternity of word, meaning and relation (Kātyāyana's first vārttika), the sphoṭa as the word with sound (dhvani) as its quality (on P 1.1.70), and whether words denote the universal or the individual (Vājapyāyana and Vyāḍi, on P 1.2.64).

title: Mahābhāṣya-pradīpa of Kaiyaṭa
summary: U31 contribution: Kaiyaṭa's commentary on the Mahābhāṣya, which reads Patañjali in the light of Bhartṛhari and transmits the sphoṭa doctrine to the later grammarians.

title: Uddyota of Nāgeśa on the Mahābhāṣya-pradīpa
summary: Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa's sub-commentary on Kaiyaṭa's Pradīpa, the standard reading of the Mahābhāṣya in the later Pāṇinian schools.

title: Sphoṭasiddhi of Maṇḍana Miśra
summary: Maṇḍana Miśra's defence of the sphoṭa in kārikās with his own commentary: the letters, each perishing, cannot convey meaning singly or together; the word is grasped as one entity manifested by the sounds, against Kumārila's view that the letters themselves (through impressions) convey meaning.

title: Gopālikā of Parameśvara on the Sphoṭasiddhi
summary: A Kerala commentary by Ṛṣiputra Parameśvara on Maṇḍana's Sphoṭasiddhi.

title: Sphoṭasiddhi of Bharata Miśra
summary: A short treatise defending the sphoṭa against the Mīmāṃsakas, distinct from Maṇḍana's work of the same name.
notes: Recalled as printed in the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series; details to verify.

title: Vaiyākaraṇa-siddhānta-kārikā of Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita
summary: Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita's short verse summary of the grammarians' doctrines on the meanings of roots, endings, nominal stems, compounds and negation, ending with the sphoṭa, where he holds that on final analysis only the sentence-sphoṭa is real.

title: Vaiyākaraṇa-bhūṣaṇa of Kauṇḍa Bhaṭṭa
summary: Kauṇḍa Bhaṭṭa's full commentary on his uncle Bhaṭṭoji's kārikās, defending the grammarians' semantics against Mīmāṃsā and Navya-Nyāya.

title: Vaiyākaraṇa-bhūṣaṇa-sāra of Kauṇḍa Bhaṭṭa
summary: The abridged Bhūṣaṇa, studied as the standard introduction to grammatical philosophy; its sections (nirṇaya) treat the meaning of roots, verbal endings, case endings, stems, compounds, the power of words (śakti), particles, and close with the settlement of the sphoṭa (sphoṭa-nirṇaya).

title: Vaiyākaraṇa-siddhānta-mañjūṣā (Bṛhanmañjūṣā) of Nāgeśa
summary: Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa's large systematic work on grammatical philosophy: the powers of words (abhidhā, lakṣaṇā, vyañjanā), sentence meaning, sphoṭa and the levels of speech.

title: Vaiyākaraṇa-siddhānta-laghumañjūṣā of Nāgeśa
summary: Nāgeśa's middle-length summary of the Mañjūṣā, the classic source for the grammarians' mapping of the four levels of speech (parā, paśyantī, madhyamā, vaikharī) onto places in the body and for the sphoṭa as identical with madhyamā-level word.

title: Paramalaghumañjūṣā of Nāgeśa
summary: Nāgeśa's shortest primer of grammatical philosophy, on the power of words (śakti), indication, suggestion and the meanings of grammatical elements.

title: Sphoṭavāda of Nāgeśa
summary: A short treatise by Nāgeśa establishing the sphoṭa against its critics.

title: Nandikeśvara-kāśikā
summary: U31 contribution: the verse commentary reading the fourteen Māheśvara sūtras (the phoneme list sounded by Śiva's drum) as teachings on the supreme and its manifestation — the letter a as the supreme Lord and the sounds as the unfolding of Śiva and Śakti; a bridge between grammar and mantra theory.

title: Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha
summary: U31 contribution: its chapter on the Pāṇini-darśana presents grammar as a school of liberation — the sphoṭa as the eternal meaning-bearer, the word-brahman, and grammar as the door to release, quoting the Vākyapadīya.

title: Tattvasaṅgraha of Śāntarakṣita
summary: U31 contribution: Śāntarakṣita's compendium of refutations (with Kamalaśīla's Pañjikā) contains a chapter examining the Word-brahman (Śabdabrahma-parīkṣā) that rejects the grammarians' claim that the world is a transformation or appearance of an eternal Word.
notes: Chapter number of the Śabdabrahma-parīkṣā not fixed here (early in the work).

title: Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa of Prabhācandra
summary: Prabhācandra's large Digambara commentary on Māṇikyanandi's Parīkṣāmukha, which among its refutations of other schools argues against the grammarians' Word-monism (śabdādvaita).
notes: Location of the śabdādvaita refutation inside the work not fixed here.

title: Śāradātilaka
summary: U31 contribution (lineage owner): the most authoritative manual of mantra-śāstra. Paṭala 1 gives the cosmogony of sound — Śakti, nāda and bindu from the supreme Lord (1.7), the threefold bindu (1.8–9), śabda-brahman as the consciousness of all beings (1.11–13), dwelling as kuṇḍalinī and manifesting as the letters (1.14) — and the fifty letters with their deities; paṭala 2 gives the classes of mantras, their fifty defects (2.64–70), the ten purifications (2.112–122), and the marks of guru and disciple and the period of testing (2.141–153); later paṭalas give the mantras, worship and puraścaraṇa of many deities, and the last paṭala treats yoga.
notes: Wording and locator checked in Phase B against a local e-text in sources_raw/; still a skeleton entry (not fidelity-checked). (paṭalas 1–2 checked in the Muktabodha M00077 e-text with the Padārthādarśa).

title: Padārthādarśa of Rāghavabhaṭṭa
summary: Rāghavabhaṭṭa's learned commentary on the Śāradātilaka, finished in Vārāṇasī in 1493/94, which quotes a very wide range of Āgamas, Tantras and Purāṇas; among them the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā's definitions of spoken, whispered and mental japa.
notes: Wording and locator checked in Phase B against a local e-text in sources_raw/; still a skeleton entry (not fidelity-checked).

title: Prapañcasāra
summary: U31 contribution (lineage owner): a mantra manual ascribed to Śaṅkara that begins with the unfolding of the world from the supreme through Śakti, sound and the letters, treats the letters (mātṛkā) and their placement, initiation, and then the mantras and worship of many deities; Rāghavabhaṭṭa and later authors cite it beside the Śāradātilaka.

title: Prapañcasāra-vivaraṇa
summary: A commentary on the Prapañcasāra ascribed by tradition to Padmapāda, Śaṅkara's disciple.

attribution.scholarly: ascription doubtful, as for the root text

title: Mantramahodadhi of Mahīdhara
summary: Mahīdhara's compendium of mantras in twenty-five 'waves' (taraṅga) with his own commentary (Naukā): mantras, meditations, yantras and puraścaraṇa of Gaṇeśa, the Goddesses, Śiva, Viṣṇu, Hanumat and others, with rules for choosing, testing and purifying mantras, and the six rites.

title: Mantramahārṇava
summary: A late encyclopaedic collection of mantras, meditations and rites arranged by deity, widely printed and used by priests.
notes: Compiler and date not recorded here (uncertain).

title: Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati
summary: U31 contribution: its Mantrapāda sets out the mantras of Śiva and other deities with their placement and rites in the Kerala Śaiva ritual tradition.

title: Nāṭyaśāstra
summary: The encyclopaedia of drama ascribed to Bharata: the origin of drama as a fifth Veda made by Brahmā for all classes (ch. 1), the theatre and the worship of the stage deities (2–3), dance (4), the preliminaries (5), rasa (6) and bhāva (7), the four kinds of acting — bodily, verbal, costume and 'sāttvika' (8–26), dramatic forms and plot (18–21), music: śrutis, svaras, grāmas, jātis, instruments and songs (28–33), characters and roles (34–35), and the descent of drama to earth (36).

attribution.tradition: taught by the sage Bharata, who received the Nāṭyaveda from Brahmā
attribution.scholarly: a compilation with older and later layers

tradition.text: made by Brahmā at the start of the Tretā age (NŚ 1.8–12)

structure.description: 36 chapters in the edition used here (37 in some recensions); verse with prose passages

editions.name: Gaekwad's Oriental Series, with the Abhinavabhāratī (4 vols)

notes: Wording and locator checked in Phase B against a local e-text in sources_raw/; still a skeleton entry (not fidelity-checked).

title: Abhinavabhāratī (Nāṭyavedavivṛti) of Abhinavagupta
summary: Abhinavagupta's commentary on the Nāṭyaśāstra, the principal source for the debate on how rasa arises: it reports and criticises Lollaṭa, Śaṅkuka and Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka and sets out Abhinava's own view of rasa as the relish (carvaṇā) of a universalized emotion in the spectator's own consciousness, the seven obstacles to it, and śānta as a rasa whose stable basis is knowledge of the self.
notes: Survives with gaps; printed in the Gaekwad's Oriental Series edition of the Nāṭyaśāstra.

title: Dhvanyāloka of Ānandavardhana
summary: The treatise that made suggestion (dhvani) the soul of poetry: besides the expressed meaning there is a 'further', implied meaning in great poets' speech (1.4), whose highest form is suggested rasa; the Rāmāyaṇa's grief become verse shows it (1.5); the Mahābhārata's principal rasa is śānta and its principal aim liberation (4.5 vṛtti).

attribution.tradition: Ānandavardhana (Abhinavagupta at places distinguishes the author of the kārikās from the author of the vṛtti)
attribution.scholarly: most take kārikās and vṛtti to be Ānandavardhana's; some ascribe the kārikās to an earlier 'Sahṛdaya'

scholarly.text: c. mid-9th c. CE (Kashmir, under Avantivarman)

title: Locana (Dhvanyālokalocana) of Abhinavagupta
summary: Abhinavagupta's commentary on the Dhvanyāloka, which ties dhvani to rasa, explains the krauñca story as the poet's grief transformed into the relishable karuṇa rasa, and argues for śānta rasa.

title: Kāvyālaṅkāra of Bhāmaha
summary: The earliest surviving independent work on poetics after Bharata: poetry is word and meaning together (1.16); figures of speech rest on 'crooked' expression (vakrokti); it also criticizes grammarians' and logicians' positions.

title: Kāvyādarśa of Daṇḍin
summary: Daṇḍin's 'mirror of poetry' in three chapters: the body of poetry, the southern (vaidarbha) and eastern (gauḍa) styles and their ten qualities, and the figures of sense and sound. Its opening praises the light called word, without which the three worlds would be blind darkness.

title: Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra(vṛtti) of Vāmana
summary: Vāmana's aphorisms with his commentary: style (rīti) is the soul of poetry (1.2.6), style being a special arrangement of words made of qualities (guṇa).

title: Kāvyālaṅkāra-sāra-saṅgraha of Udbhaṭa
summary: Udbhaṭa's classification of figures of speech; the first to bring rasa into the figure called rasavat with the language of vibhāva and sthāyin.

title: Kāvyālaṅkāra of Rudraṭa
summary: Rudraṭa's treatise in sixteen chapters on figures, faults and rasa; it counts ten rasas, adding śānta and preyas ('affection') to Bharata's eight. Commented on by the Jain Namisādhu (1069).
notes: The chapter giving the ten rasas is not fixed here.

title: Hṛdayadarpaṇa of Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka
summary: Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka's lost work on poetics, known through Abhinavagupta and Mahimabhaṭṭa: poetry's language has, beyond denotation, the powers of 'making present' (bhāvakatva) and 'making enjoyable' (bhojakatva), by which rasa is enjoyed in a state of sattva akin to tasting Brahman.

title: Kāvyakautuka of Bhaṭṭa Tauta
summary: The lost work on poetics and drama of Abhinavagupta's teacher Bhaṭṭa Tauta, known from Abhinava's citations; it is credited with the view that the experience of the hero, the poet and the spectator is the same.

title: Vakroktijīvita of Kuntaka
summary: Kuntaka's theory that 'striking, oblique expression' (vakrokti) is the life of poetry, analysed at six levels from the phoneme to the whole work.

title: Vyaktiviveka of Mahimabhaṭṭa
summary: Mahimabhaṭṭa's critique of the theory of suggestion: what Ānandavardhana calls dhvani is inference (anumāna); there is only one power of words, denotation.

title: Daśarūpaka of Dhanañjaya
summary: Dhanañjaya's manual of the ten forms of drama, plot, characters and rasa; it treats rasa as arising in the spectator from the determinants and denies that śānta can be a rasa in drama.

scholarly.text: late 10th c. CE (court of Muñja of Mālava)

title: Avaloka of Dhanika on the Daśarūpaka
summary: Dhanika's commentary on his brother Dhanañjaya's Daśarūpaka, arguing that rasa is apprehended through the sentence's purport (tātparya) and not by a separate power of suggestion.

title: Śṛṅgāraprakāśa of Bhoja
summary: King Bhoja's vast work on poetics in thirty-six chapters, holding that there is in truth one rasa, śṛṅgāra understood as self-regard (abhimāna, ahaṃkāra), of which the named rasas are developments.

title: Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa (on poetics) of Bhoja
summary: Bhoja's compendium of poetics in five chapters (distinct from his grammar of the same name).

title: Aucityavicāracarcā of Kṣemendra
summary: Kṣemendra's essay making propriety (aucitya) the life of rasa-filled poetry, illustrated with good and bad examples.

title: Kāvyaprakāśa of Mammaṭa
summary: Mammaṭa's synthesis of poetics in ten chapters: the purposes and causes of poetry (1.2–3), its definition as faultless word and meaning with qualities (1.4), the three powers of words (denotation, indication, suggestion), rasa and bhāva (ch. 4) — love toward a deity is a bhāva, not a rasa — and śānta as the ninth rasa with dispassion as its stable emotion; the most commented work of the tradition.
notes: Wording and locator checked in Phase B against a local e-text in sources_raw/; still a skeleton entry (not fidelity-checked).

title: Alaṅkārasarvasva of Ruyyaka
summary: Ruyyaka's systematic treatment of the figures of speech within the dhvani framework.

title: Sāhityadarpaṇa of Viśvanātha Kavirāja
summary: Viśvanātha's comprehensive manual in ten chapters: poetry is a sentence whose soul is rasa (1.3); rasa is the stable emotion made relishable by determinants, consequents and transient states (3.1), undivided, self-luminous, bliss and consciousness, twin of tasting Brahman (3.2); śānta (3.245–250) and vatsala ('parental affection', 3.251) are also rasas.
notes: Wording and locator checked in Phase B against a local e-text in sources_raw/; still a skeleton entry (not fidelity-checked). (GRETIL kārikā text, ed. Satyavrata Simha 1992).

title: Rasagaṅgādhara of Jagannātha Paṇḍitarāja
summary: Jagannātha's late, incomplete masterpiece (two ānanas): poetry is a word expressing a charming meaning; rasa is consciousness itself, its veil removed, delimited by the stable emotion.

scholarly.text: mid-17th c. CE (Mughal court and Vārāṇasī)

title: Kāvyamīmāṃsā of Rājaśekhara
summary: Rājaśekhara's 'inquiry into poetry', of which only the first of eighteen planned books survives: the myth of the Poetry-Man (kāvyapuruṣa) born of Sarasvatī, the kinds of poetic genius (pratibhā) — creative (kārayitrī) and appreciative (bhāvayitrī) — and the poet's training and daily routine.

title: Nāṭyadarpaṇa of Rāmacandra and Guṇacandra
summary: A Jain dramaturgical treatise by two disciples of Hemacandra, notable for holding that rasa is of the nature of both pleasure and pain (sukha-duḥkhātmaka), against the view that every rasa is bliss.

title: Kāvyānuśāsana of Hemacandra
summary: Hemacandra's Jain manual of poetics with his own commentaries (Alaṅkāracūḍāmaṇi, Viveka), largely following Mammaṭa and Abhinavagupta on rasa.

title: Bhāvaprakāśana of Śāradātanaya
summary: Śāradātanaya's treatise on bhāva, rasa and drama, gathering many earlier views.

title: Abhinayadarpaṇa of Nandikeśvara
summary: A short manual of dance and gesture (hand-gestures, glances, head and neck movements) ascribed to Nandikeśvara, basic to classical dance teaching; it states that where the hand goes the eye follows, the mind follows the eye, feeling (bhāva) the mind, and rasa arises from feeling.

title: Uttararāmacarita of Bhavabhūti
summary: Bhavabhūti's drama on Rāma's later life, famous for the verse that there is only one rasa, compassion (karuṇa), which appears as different rasas as water appears as eddies, bubbles and waves (3.47).

title: Nāradīya Śikṣā
summary: U31 contribution: the Sāmaveda's phonetic manual is also the oldest source of the music tradition's notes — it sets the seven Sāman notes against the flute's notes (1.5.1–2), gives the animal cries of the notes (1.5.3–4), the grāmas and mūrchanās, and the places of the notes in the body.

title: Dattilam
summary: Dattila's concise verse treatise on gāndharva music — śruti, svara, grāma, mūrchanā, tāna, jāti and tāla — closely related to the Nāṭyaśāstra's music chapters.

title: Bṛhaddeśī of Mataṅga
summary: Mataṅga's treatise on 'regional' (deśī) music: the teaching on nāda — without nāda there is no song, note or dance; the world is made of nāda; Brahmā, Janārdana, the supreme Śakti and Maheśvara are nāda-forms (16–18); nāda arises in the 'place of Brahmā' from the union of breath and fire (18–22) and is fivefold (23–25) — then śrutis, svaras, grāmas, jātis and the first definition of rāga as the sound-pattern that colours the minds of people (280–281).
notes: Wording and locator checked in Phase B against a local e-text in sources_raw/; still a skeleton entry (not fidelity-checked). Verse numbers follow the eBhāratī e-text.

title: Bharatabhāṣya (Sarasvatīhṛdayālaṅkāra) of Nānyadeva
summary: King Nānyadeva's commentary-treatise on the music of the Nāṭyaśāstra, a bridge between Mataṅga and Śārṅgadeva.

title: Saṅgītaratnākara of Śārṅgadeva
summary: The standard treatise of Indian music in seven chapters (svara, rāga, miscellany, compositions, tāla, instruments, dance). Its first chapter opens with the worship of nāda-brahman and a section on the 'origin of the body' (piṇḍotpatti): Brahman and the jīvas, creation, embryology, the channels and ten centres of the body — the jīva's place on certain petals bringing success or failure in song — and the teaching that the struck nāda, delighting people, breaks the bondage of existence; then the origin of nāda from breath and fire, the twenty-two śrutis and seven svaras.

scholarly.text: c. 1210–1247 CE (Yādava court of Siṅghaṇa, Devagiri)

structure.description: 7 adhyāyas: svaragata, rāgaviveka, prakīrṇaka, prabandha, tāla, vādya, nartana

editions.name: Adyar Library edition with the commentaries of Kallinātha and Siṃhabhūpāla
R. K. Shringy and Prem Lata Sharma, English translation

notes: Wording and locator checked in Phase B against a local e-text in sources_raw/; still a skeleton entry (not fidelity-checked).

title: Kalānidhi of Kallinātha on the Saṅgītaratnākara
summary: Kallinātha's commentary on the Saṅgītaratnākara, written at the Vijayanagara court, relating the treatise to the practice of his time.

title: Saṅgītasudhākara of Siṃhabhūpāla on the Saṅgītaratnākara
summary: Siṃhabhūpāla's commentary on the Saṅgītaratnākara.

title: Saṅgītasamayasāra of Pārśvadeva
summary: A Jain author's treatise on music, including regional songs and instruments of his time.
notes: Sectarian affiliation (Digambara) recalled with low confidence.

title: Mānasollāsa (Abhilaṣitārthacintāmaṇi) of Someśvara III
summary: The Cālukya king Someśvara III's encyclopaedia of royal pleasures, whose sections on song, instrument and dance (gīta-vinoda etc.) are an important record of music before Śārṅgadeva.

title: Saṅgītarāja of Kumbhakarṇa
summary: Mahārāṇā Kumbhā of Mewar's large music encyclopaedia.

title: Svaramelakalānidhi of Rāmāmātya
summary: Rāmāmātya's treatise classifying rāgas under parent scales (mela).

title: Rāgavibodha of Somanātha
summary: Somanātha's treatise on the classification and ornamentation of rāgas on the vīṇā.

title: Caturdaṇḍīprakāśikā of Veṅkaṭamakhin
summary: Veṅkaṭamakhin's treatise that sets out the scheme of seventy-two parent scales (melakarta), the basis of later Karṇāṭaka rāga classification.

title: Saṅgītasudhā of Govinda Dīkṣita
summary: A music treatise ascribed to Govinda Dīkṣita (or to the Nāyaka king Raghunātha) of Tanjore.

title: Saṅgītapārijāta of Ahobala
summary: Ahobala's treatise, notable for defining the positions of the notes on the length of the vīṇā string.

title: Saṅgītadarpaṇa of Dāmodara
summary: Dāmodara's widely used compendium of music, largely drawing on the Saṅgītaratnākara, with the rāga-rāginī imagery of the northern tradition.

title: Ṣaḍrāgacandrodaya of Puṇḍarīka Viṭṭhala
summary: One of Puṇḍarīka Viṭṭhala's treatises on the rāgas of the northern tradition.
